title: Hormuz closure: the maritime risk-transfer and rerouting chain beneath the oil price
map_limitation: Four blind spots specific to THIS map. (1) The root is unbuyable and publishes nothing: the strait is held by the IRGC and the transit charge was run by the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, an Iranian body the United States sanctioned, which never published a fee schedule. Every toll figure on this map is a third-party estimate, hormuz-transit-control carries zero tickers by design, and the pool the appraisal identified as the largest by rate of collection has no instrument at any price. (2) The two layers this occurrence repriced hardest are structurally unlisted, so supplier-side EDGAR full-text search cannot reach them. The liability half of marine war risk is written by mutuals with no equity at all (Gard, Skuld, NorthStandard, the London P&I Club, the American Club and the rest of the International Group), the intelligence and protection layer is private (Ambrey, Constellis, Dryad Global, Risk Intelligence, Kpler, Windward, Lloyd's List Intelligence), the bunker names expanding into the Cape trade are private (Monjasa, Vitol, Bunker Partner, Peninsula, Flex Commodities, Global Fuel Supply), the manning agencies paying the war bonuses are private, and the bypass pipelines are state assets. maritime-risk-and-protection therefore carries one ticker and crew-and-warlike-area-manning carries none, and that is a finding about the chain, not a gap in the search. (3) The listed names that matter mostly file outside the SEC and reach this map through research rather than through fts: BEZ.L, HSX.L, LRE.L, ALV.DE, ZURN.SW, 8766.T, 8725.T, MUV2.DE, SREN.SW, HNR1.DE, SCR.PA, OET.OL, TRMD-A.CO, HAFN.OL, 9104.T, 9101.T, 1138.HK, FLNG.OL, MAERSK-B.CO, HLAG.DE, 2603.TW, 2609.TW, 011200.KS, 601919.SS, 2222.SR, VPK.AS, EXA.PA, SAAB-B.ST, KOG.OL, HO.PA, LDO.MI, BA.L, FCT.MI, EQNR.OL, WDS.AX, RELIANCE.NS, IOC.NS, 5020.T, 010950.KS, 0386.HK, TOP.BK, 9531.T, SHEL.L, BP.L and TTE.PA. (4) Three quantities the thesis rests on are directionally sourced and quantitatively soft. Every freight rate here is a trade-press print of an LSEG or Baltic assessment quoted secondhand, not a fetched series, so no rate on this map can be re-derived in this repo. War-risk premium is a broker-quoted percentage of hull value with a 1% to 10% spread across the cited sources, and no issuer discloses Gulf war-risk premium income separately, so the split between the primary book, the reinsurance layer and the state backstop cannot be sized from any filing. And the Joint War Committee's listed areas now cover the Red Sea and the Gulf together, while no cited source splits premium or claims between this occurrence and the pre-existing Houthi book, which makes double-counting the two the most likely quiet error on this map.

links.name: Hormuz transit control and the Iranian toll regime
links.role: The disruption itself and this map's uninvestable root: the IRGC holds the strait closed and conditions reopening on a political settlement, and for the transits it did allow it charged individual vessels through a state authority, so every downstream link's volume, risk premium and freight rate is set by a party no brokerage account can reach.

evidence.claim: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it would reopen the Strait of Hormuz only if the United States stops obstructing and returns to the memorandum, making reopening conditional on a political settlement rather than on shipping conditions.
evidence.source_name: The Washington Times, Iran says the Strait of Hormuz stays closed until the U.S. meets its terms
source_excerpt: If the United States stops obstructing and returns to the memorandum, we can reopen the Strait of Hormuz within the framework of the agreement.

evidence.claim: Iran's wartime Hormuz transit charge ran roughly $1 million to $2 million per vessel, per voyage, scaled to the size of the ship, the type of cargo and the volume carried; Iran did not publish a fee schedule, and the United States responded by sanctioning the entity administering the charges.
evidence.source_name: Straits, Strait of Hormuz Transit Fee: Iran's Hormuz Toll, Explained
source_excerpt: roughly $1 million to $2 million per vessel, per voyage, with the exact figure scaled to the size of the ship, the type of cargo, and the volume carried.
Iran did not publish a fee schedule.
The United States responded by sanctioning the Iranian entity administering the charges, treating the toll apparatus itself as a target rather than recognizing it as a legitimate fee for service.
evidence.note: Continuously updated reference page; source_date is the access date for this run, not a fixed publication date.

evidence.claim: The Joint Maritime Information Center recorded maritime attacks involving commercial vessels and offshore infrastructure across the Arabian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman, which is the physical mechanism keeping the route closed.
evidence.source_name: Lloyd's Market Association, Safety concerns, not insurance availability, driving reduced vessel traffic in the Strait of Hormuz
source_excerpt: 23 maritime attacks involving commercial vessels and offshore infrastructure reported across the Arabian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman.

evidence.claim: The closure drove the United States government to create a Gulf maritime war-risk reinsurance facility through the International Development Finance Corporation, with Chubb as lead underwriter managing the facility, determining pricing and terms, assuming risk and issuing policies, structured as a public-private partnership in which other American insurers act as reinsurers.
evidence.source_name: Insurance Journal, Chubb Outlines Structure of $20B Gulf Reinsurance Facility, Now Including Liability Cover
source_excerpt: Chubb, acting as lead underwriter, will manage the facility, determine pricing and terms, assume risk, and issue policies for eligible vessels and cargo.
a public-private partnership between DFC, Chubb, and other name-brand American insurance companies who will act as reinsurers.

evidence.claim: The closure created a persistent advisory and monitoring requirement: vessel movements remain below historical levels and operators continue to face a combination of security threats, navigation hazards and operational uncertainty.
evidence.source_name: Skuld, Maritime security update: Gulf Region / Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea
source_excerpt: vessel movements remain below historical levels and operators continue to face a combination of security threats, navigation hazards and operational uncertainty

evidence.claim: The closure triggered a state mine-clearance response: CENTCOM said it had begun the process of establishing a new passage and would share the safe pathway with the maritime industry to encourage the free flow of commerce.
evidence.source_name: DefenseScoop, Navy to use underwater drones to help clear Iranian mines from Strait of Hormuz
source_excerpt: Today, we began the process of establishing a new passage and we will share this safe pathway with the maritime industry soon to encourage the free flow of commerce.

evidence.claim: The closure moved marine fuel demand out of the Gulf and onto the Cape route, and fuel oil supply is expected to tighten across all bunkering hubs.

source_excerpt: Volumes have been positively impacted by the Red Sea security situation causing more vessels to reroute south of Africa
fuel oil supply is expected to tighten across all bunkering hubs.

evidence.claim: The closure turned crewing into a priced constraint: at least 59 commercial ships have come under attack in and around the Persian Gulf since the war began at the end of February, with 17 seafarers losing their lives.
evidence.source_name: Transport Topics, Shipowners Offer Huge Bonuses to Get Crews to Sail Hormuz
source_excerpt: At least 59 commercial ships have come under attack in and around the Persian Gulf since the war began at the end of February, with 17 seafarers losing their lives.

evidence.claim: The volume the closure removed is the reason the bypass lines matter: around 20 million barrels of crude and oil products transit the strait each day, as well as roughly a fifth of global liquefied natural gas exports, against existing bypass capacity of around 3.5 million barrels to 5.5 million barrels a day of crude capacity.
evidence.source_name: The Conversation, What alternatives do Gulf states have to the Strait of Hormuz?
source_excerpt: around 20 million barrels of crude and oil products each day, as well as roughly a fifth of global liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.
around 3.5 million barrels to 5.5 million barrels a day of crude capacity

evidence.claim: The closure removed over 10 billion cubic feet per day of global LNG supplies, or approximately 20%, which is the gap non-Gulf exporters are being asked to fill.
evidence.source_name: U.S. Energy Information Administration, International LNG prices rise amid Strait of Hormuz closure
source_excerpt: over 10 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) of global LNG supplies, or approximately 20%

bottleneck.note: ARCH-003 inverted, the same shape as russian-diesel-ban/russian-refining-attrition: this link sets every other link's volume and price and there is no instrument for it at any price. The IRGC and the Persian Gulf Strait Authority are sanctioned and file nothing, so the ticker list is deliberately empty.

capture_inputs.supply_concentration: Total and entirely outside the investable set. One party controls transit and priced it case by case with no published schedule.
capture_inputs.substitutability: None for the waterway itself. The only physical alternative is the bypass pipeline capacity at hormuz-bypass-pipelines, cited at around 3.5 to 5.5 million barrels a day against around 20 million barrels a day of normal transit, and there is no pipeline alternative at all for LNG.
capture_inputs.who_posted_the_margin: The toll collector, and the estimated collection rate is the largest single identified pool in this occurrence's impact appraisal. Nobody on this link is reachable, which is precisely why the appraisal scored public_reach 50 and banded the occurrence LEAKY.

links.name: War-risk reinsurance capacity and the state backstop
links.role: The balance sheet that has to exist before any hull can be covered: the reinsurance and retrocession lines standing behind the marine war account, plus the two capacity vehicles the closure forced into being, the US government facility led by Chubb and the Lloyd's market consortium.

evidence.claim: The US International Development Finance Corporation created a $20 billion Gulf marine war-risk reinsurance facility with Chubb as lead underwriter, covering war hull risk insurance, war P&I insurance and war cargo insurance.
evidence.source_name: Insurance Journal, Chubb Outlines Structure of $20B Gulf Reinsurance Facility, Now Including Liability Cover
source_excerpt: The maritime insurance facility was created by the U.S. government via the U.S. International Development Finance Corp. (DFC), which on March 11 announced Chubb as lead underwriter for its $20 billion reinsurance plan.
war marine risk insurance for hull & liability as well as cargo. Coverage will be offered for war hull risk insurance, for war P&I insurance and war cargo insurance.

evidence.claim: Lloyd's launched a market consortium providing additional marine war risk insurance capacity for vessels and cargo transiting the Strait of Hormuz, with Chubb serving as lead underwriter supported by participating Lloyd's syndicates, providing up to $200 million of capacity separately for hull and P&I risks with an additional $200 million of dedicated cargo capacity.
evidence.source_name: Lloyd's, Launch of new marine war risk consortium to support Strait of Hormuz shipping
source_excerpt: Today, Lloyd's welcomed the launch of a new Lloyd's market consortium designed to provide additional marine war risk insurance capacity for vessels and cargo transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
Chubb will serve as lead underwriter, supported by participating Lloyd's syndicates and specialist market partners.
It will provide up to $200 million of capacity separately for hull and P&I risks, with an additional $200 million of dedicated cargo capacity.

evidence.claim: Reinsurance terms set what the primary war book can charge: after the Gulf war-risk withdrawals marine hull rates were set to rise 25-50%, and war-risk premiums that were around 0.25% of vessel value increased multiple times, limiting the commercial viability of transit.
evidence.source_name: Reinsurance Business, War-risk withdrawals and rate hikes pressure Gulf reinsurance market
source_excerpt: marine hull rates set to rise 25-50%
War-risk premiums that were around 0.25% of vessel value have increased multiple times, limiting the commercial viability of transit.
reinsurers are repricing exposures across marine, aviation, energy, and political violence lines while maintaining coverage continuity.

bottleneck.note: Capacity was scarce enough that a government and a market consortium both had to manufacture it, which is the tell for HIGH. Not CHOKE_POINT: the Lloyd's Market Association's own survey says appetite never disappeared, so the binding constraint sat at crew and vessel safety, not at capital.

capture_inputs.supply_concentration: Concentrated by construction on this occurrence: one named lead underwriter, Chubb, sits at the head of both cited capacity vehicles, the $20 billion government facility and the $200 million per line Lloyd's consortium.
capture_inputs.substitutability: Low in the acute phase. Cited reinsurers reduced line sizes on Middle East exposed treaties rather than replacing withdrawn capacity, which is why a sovereign balance sheet had to be inserted.
capture_inputs.who_posted_the_margin: Undisclosed. No cited issuer breaks out Gulf war-risk premium income, and the state facility absorbs an unpublished share of the risk, so the margin actually earned on this layer cannot be read from any source on this map.
capture_inputs.shared_bom: CB appears on this link and on marine-war-risk-underwriting: one issuer wearing two link labels, not two bets. Separately, this is the ONE link this chain shares with the offshore-counter-drone chain being built in parallel: the Lloyd's and reinsurance capital layer is common to both, but this chain's underwriting is war risk on MOVING HULLS (war hull, war P&I, war cargo) while that chain's is fixed offshore installations, a different policy and a different loss model.

links.name: Marine war-risk underwriting on moving hulls
links.role: The primary war book this occurrence repriced: hull war, war P&I and war cargo written on vessels under way through the strait, by Lloyd's syndicates, the mutual P&I clubs and the large composite insurers, and distinct from the fixed offshore installation book that shares the same reinsurance layer.

capture_inputs.supply_concentration: The cited P&I withdrawals were simultaneous across Gard, Skuld, NorthStandard, the London P&I Club and the American Club, which is the behaviour of a concentrated market acting on one reinsurance signal rather than of independent competitors.

capture_inputs.supply_concentration: The cited quotes for this occurrence come from three of the four global brokers, Aon, Marsh and Gallagher, which is the shape of an oligopoly rather than a fragmented market.

capture_inputs.who_posted_the_margin: Not established here. Commission scales with premium, and premium on this route rose by a documented multiple, but no cited source sizes the marine war revenue line at any of the listed brokers, so the earnings effect is directional only.

bottleneck.note: ARCH-004 in its logistics-dominant form: bunker fuel is fungible, so criticality comes entirely from where you can buy it. The Cape route created local pricing power at hubs that had none, which is the same mechanism that made cement regional on tibet-mega-dam.

capture_inputs.substitutability: The fuel is a commodity and fully substitutable in grade. What is not substitutable is the geography: a Cape-routed vessel cannot buy in Fujairah.
capture_inputs.logistics_or_qualification: The cited constraint is physical supply reaching the new hubs, with fuel oil supply expected to tighten across all bunkering hubs, which is the condition that turns a commodity into a local monopoly for a season.
capture_inputs.who_posted_the_margin: The named firms expanding into African bunkering in the cited source are private traders and suppliers, not the listed majors on this ticker list. That gap is the reason this link is PARTIAL and why its capture is likely lower than its volume.

Named by the Lloyd's Market Association as the actual reason tonnage stopped moving, ahead of insurance capacity, which is this map's single most important correction to the signal's thesis. capture_inputs.supply_concentration: None. Labour supply is global and fragmented, and the price moved by a documented multiple anyway, which is what happens when supply is willing rather than scarce.

capture_inputs.who_posted_the_margin: Nobody. The bonus is a pure cost transfer from the tanker owner to the seafarer, so it is a drag on crude-tanker-tonnage's realised margin that the headline freight rate does not show.

bottleneck.note: The one CHOKE_POINT on this map with deep listed coverage, and the reason is time rather than steel: a third of effective capacity is absorbed by voyage length and cannot be replaced inside the horizon, because the fleet is fixed and the detour is not optional. The screen's job here is to separate the owners with spot exposure from those on long charter, because the same headline rate reaches them very differently.

capture_inputs.supply_concentration: Fragmented ownership, but the binding scarcity is not ownership share, it is that the cited fleet of roughly 800 crude VLCCs cannot grow inside the window while each voyage consumes about a third more time.
capture_inputs.substitutability: None on the route: the cargo must move by sea and the detour is compulsory while the strait is shut. That is why the price moved by a documented multiple rather than a margin.
capture_inputs.logistics_or_qualification: The detour itself is the qualification: the extra 14 days per leg is what converts a competitive freight market into a seller's market for a season.
capture_inputs.who_posted_the_margin: Here, visibly, and the cited record daily rate is the evidence. But three links upstream are costs against it that the headline rate does not net out: the war premium, the bunker uplift on a 56 percent longer voyage, and the crew bonus.

Cargoes are not moving because Ras Laffan is loading fewer of them, so a carrier owner captures the ton-mile stretch on the cargoes that do move and loses the ones that do not.

capture_inputs.logistics_or_qualification: LNG carriers are purpose-built and chartered long, so a spot rate spike reaches fewer owners here than it does on crude tankers.
capture_inputs.who_posted_the_margin: Split and unresolved by the sources on this map: the price move landed on the benchmark, not visibly on the carrier owner, and no cited source attributes the TTF or JKM move to shipping economics rather than to lost molecules.
capture_inputs.shared_bom: 9104.T and 9101.T also appear on crude-tanker-tonnage. Those two Japanese owners are one exposure to this occurrence across two links, not two.

capture_inputs.substitutability: High at the route level: a liner can omit the Gulf entirely and still run its Asia to Europe string, which is exactly what the cited End of Voyage declaration is.
capture_inputs.logistics_or_qualification: The cited trapped tonnage is the real constraint, because 138 ships inside a closed Gulf is capacity that cannot serve any other trade.
capture_inputs.who_posted_the_margin: The surcharge is a posted tariff and the sources here do not show whether it was collected in full, so this link's capture is asserted by the carriers rather than demonstrated by the evidence.

links.role: The only physical way around the strait for crude: Saudi Arabia's East-West line to Yanbu and the Abu Dhabi line to Fujairah, together able to carry a fraction of normal transit, and constrained by export terminals rather than by pipe.

capture_inputs.substitutability: This link IS the substitute, and it is capped: the cited bypass capacity replaces roughly a fifth to a quarter of normal transit and nothing at all of the LNG.
capture_inputs.logistics_or_qualification: The binding constraint is the export terminal, not the pipe. The cited pipeline ceiling exceeds what the Red Sea loading point can sustain, which is why more pipe does not automatically mean more barrels.
capture_inputs.who_posted_the_margin: The state owner. The expansion is a roughly $3 billion construction programme, which is ARCH-002 in miniature: real volume, competitively bid, and too small to carry its own link on this map.

links.name: Non-Gulf supply substitution
links.role: ARCH-006 in its investable form: the cargoes that replace the ones the strait no longer passes, produced and shipped by companies listed a long way from where the war is, and the part of this occurrence a brokerage account can most cleanly reach.

capture_inputs.substitutability: The buyer is substituting away from the Gulf, which is the whole point, but the cited concentration of world LNG trade in three exporting countries means the substitution runs through a narrow set of sellers.
capture_inputs.logistics_or_qualification: The binding constraint is liquefaction capacity and its permitting, not molecules, and the cited 2.4 Bcf/d arriving through 2026 is the only near-term relief.

notes.text: THE THESIS WAS TESTED AND IT SURVIVES WITH ONE STRUCTURAL CORRECTION. The signal names four unmapped layers: tanker rerouting and ton-mile, marine war-risk underwriting and the reinsurance behind it, the Persian Gulf Strait Authority transit toll, and the private maritime-security layer. All four are on this map and all four cite separately. The correction is that a fifth layer sits above three of them and nobody in the coverage names it: crew consent. The Lloyd's Market Association, surveying its own underwriters, states in terms that the reason ships are not moving is not a lack of insurance but the risk to crew and vessel safety as assessed by masters and owners, with 88% of respondents still willing to write hull war risk. The world's largest supertanker owner is separately reported offering six months' extra pay for a one-month round trip, and crews are still refusing. So the binding constraint on this chain is not underwriting capacity, which is what the insurance framing implies; it is willingness to sail. That is why crew-and-warlike-area-manning is a CHOKE_POINT with zero tickers and why marine-war-risk-underwriting is HIGH rather than CHOKE_POINT.

FLOWS ARE KEPT SEPARATE FROM REVENUES, per the appraisal's refusal to round the money leg up on a trade-flow figure. Three numbers on this map are flows and are never treated as pools: around 20 million barrels a day of transit, roughly a fifth of world LNG, and 470,000 TEUs of trapped container capacity. Three are collected revenues or committed capacity and are treated as such: the $20 billion DFC facility, the $200 million per line Lloyd's consortium, and the freight and premium prints (a record $647,000 a day Gulf-to-Asia, war risk at 7.5 to 10 percent of hull value, $77.96 a tonne of crude, a $3,000/FEU box surcharge). The toll sits in a third category and is named as such on hormuz-transit-control: a real collection with no instrument.

SHARED LINK DECLARED. war-risk-reinsurance-capacity is the one link this chain shares with offshore-counter-drone (rank 9, built separately): the Lloyd's syndicate and reinsurance capital layer is common to both. The books are NOT the same and the maps must not merge them. This chain's underwriting link, marine-war-risk-underwriting, is war risk on MOVING HULLS: war hull, war P&I and war cargo on vessels under way, listed by the Joint War Committee, cancellable at seven days' notice and repriced per voyage. offshore-counter-drone covers FIXED offshore installations, which is an energy and property book with a different loss model and a different renewal cycle. The only genuine overlap is the retrocession and Lloyd's capacity behind both, plus one issuer: CB appears on this chain twice already and is likely to appear on that one too, so a position in Chubb is one bet on the Gulf, not three.

ARCHETYPES. Applied: ARCH-003 (uninvestable order-book owner, inverted) on hormuz-transit-control, the third chain in a row where the root of the map is a sanctioned or state party that publishes nothing; ARCH-006 (geopolitical counter-response as a first-class link) twice, on naval-escort-and-mine-clearance and on non-gulf-energy-substitution, which takes ARCH-006 to its second chain and is the recurrence its Watch note was asking for; ARCH-004 (critical material, criticality equals substitutability times logistics) on bunker-and-voyage-services in its logistics-dominant form, the same mechanism that made cement regional on tibet-mega-dam; ARCH-002 (volume without capture) checked and NOT built as a link, because the only EPC scope here is a roughly $3 billion pipeline expansion that cannot carry a link of its own, so it is recorded inside hormuz-bypass-pipelines instead. Checked and did not fire: ARCH-001 (precision manufacturing capacity as the gating step), because the capacity that gates this chain is voyage time on an existing fleet and not a production line, and no cited source ties this occurrence to shipyard ordering; ARCH-005 (power and grid equipment behind someone else's story), no grid layer on this map; ARCH-007 (semis as a leaf), the nearest analogue is the satellite and analytics layer, which is folded into maritime-risk-and-protection rather than given a compute link it does not deserve.

STAGES CHECKED AND NOT BUILT, each because nothing citable tied it to this occurrence. (1) Shipyard and newbuild capacity: the fleet response to a third of capacity being absorbed by voyage length would normally be ordering, and no fetched source connects Hormuz to tanker ordering, so it is not a stage on this map. (2) Kidnap-and-ransom and hijack response: the Somali hijackings with reported multi-million dollar ransom demands imply a K&R and negotiation market, and the one article that would have established it returned HTTP 403, so it stays out rather than being cited from a search snippet. (3) Floating storage and ship-to-ship transfer: plausible from the reported hundreds of vessels anchored off Gulf coasts, but no fetched source establishes it as a commercial stage with its own economics. (4) Transshipment hub substitution away from Jebel Ali: named in liner coverage but never quantified in anything that opened. (5) Marine war-risk claims adjusting and salvage: no cited source establishes claims activity at all, which is itself the finding, because premium with no visible claims is the thing the heat stage most needs to test. Four URLs were fetched and refused: the World Economic Forum's insurers-of-last-resort piece (403), S&P Global's Marsh premium report (403), CNBC's Somali piracy and maritime-drone articles (403), and Splash247 on armed guard pricing (403). The Howden Re reinsurance report returned an unreadable PDF and was not cited. None of those five refused pages contributed a link or an edge.

Every link and every edge carries dated cited evidence with a verbatim source_excerpt from a page fetched this run. heat null on every link and scenarios empty, as the chain stage requires.
